children: Crude oil futures turned higher Wednesday following five sessions of losses, with Brent crude bouncing nearly 4%, after Iran's President Pezeshkian delivered a defiant speech at the United Nations that highlighted the wide gap with the U.S. after nearly seven months of war.

Pezeshkian said Iran would not surrender to threats and described several conditions before any meaningful talks with the U.S. could resume, a day after President Trump warned he could "annihilate" Iran.

But U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff said in a post on X that American officials had engaged in lengthy talks with the Iranian delegation through mediators on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York.
U.S. diesel futures fell after U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the Trump administration is considering implementing restrictions on diesel imports but not an outright ban.
"The blunt tool ​of banning diesel exports definitely doesn't work," Wright said at an event in New York on Wednesday.

"If you can't ⁠export the diesel that comes out of our refineries, you run out of places to store it, and you have to reduce U.S. refining, which would ​put upward pressure on gasoline prices and jet fuel prices," Wright said.

The Trump administration is working with the refining industry to increase the supply of U.S. diesel in a "simpler, voluntary, cooperative fashion, without using blunt instruments that would reduce refining throughput," Wright said, adding that policy announcements will be made in the coming days.

President Trump said Tuesday that the administration was considering restricting diesel exports, alarming the oil and gas industry that has warned a ban risked creating a series of unintended consequences that would choke supplies of diesel and gasoline in the U.S. and lead to higher prices.
Average retail diesel prices in the U.S. were $6.52/gal on Wednesday, up 76% Y/Y, according to AAA.
Meanwhile, U.S. crude oil inventories rose unexpectedly last week and refineries ran at a slower pace, according to data released by the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Commercial crude oil stocks excluding the Strategic Petroleum Reserve rose by 3M barrels to 426.4M barrels in the week ended September 18 and were 2% above the five-year average for the time of year, the EIA

U.S. crude oil production was estimated at 13.9M bbl/day, little changed from the previous week, and refineries ran at 94% of capacity, down from 96.8%, with crude input to refineries falling by 519K bbl/day to 16.8M bbl/day.

U.S. gasoline inventories fell by 1.7M barrels to 206M barrels and were 6% below the five-year average, and distillate fuel stocks fell by 428K barrels to 107.4M barrels and were 12% below the five-year average for the time of year.

The unexpected increase in U.S. crude oil stockpiles as exports fell and refineries cut runs is "slightly bearish" for crude but keeps upward pressure on gasoline prices, David Russell of TradeStation said in a note.
"Energy markets are tight but stabilizing, but it might be hard for crude to go much lower, given the record crack spreads," Russell wrote.
